newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: After Cambodia violence, Hun Sen calls for polls.
newsitem.headline: After Cambodia violence, Hun Sen calls for polls.

text.p: A week after deposing his senior rival in two days of bloody fighting, Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen said on Sunday that the country must have a free and fair election.
In a statement read by an announcer on national radio, Hun Sen gave no date for the poll.

Last month he agreed with First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, the man he ousted, that a general election should be held on May 23 next year, exactly five years after U.N.-organised polls that led to their coalition.
"It is necessary...to ensure a free and fair general election, which is the aim of all of us," the statement said.

As Hun Sen's announcement was being read out, troops loyal to him continued their pursuit of opposition forces comprising leftist Khmer Rouge guerrillas and troops loyal to Ranariddh in the northwest, not far from the temples of Angkor, Cambodia's main tourist attraction.

Reporters at the scene saw heavily armed government infantrymen streaming along national Route 6 about 50 km (30 miles) outside the town of Siem Reap, pursuing their rapidly fleeing adversaries backed by rocket and artillery fire.
Hun Sen said active steps were under way to reopen the National Assembly, which did not resume its scheduled session in April due to rows between Hun Sen and Ranariddh.
The assembly needs to pass key election laws quickly if the poll is to be held in May, political analysts say.
Hun Sen also called on all Cambodian newspapers, including those critical of him, to resume publication.
"As for the press, including newspapers that used to be critical, please hurry and publish," his statement said.
Some Cambodians newspapers, including many that supported Ranariddh, ceased publication during the two days of fighting in Phnom Penh and subsequent looting and chaos.
Many members of Ranariddh's party, as well as thousands of foreign business people and aid workers, fled Cambodia on emergency evacuation flights after the prince's ouster.
At least 58 people were killed and up to 200 wounded in the fighting. Most of the casualties were civilians.
Major foreign governments have condemned the violence and some have suspended or are reconsidering their aid programmes.
Ranariddh has sought the support of the international community since his ouster and called on governments not to recognise any administration resulting from his overthrow.
An Asian diplomat in Phnom Penh said that by making the statement about free and fair elections Hun Sen was aiming to restore his image at home and abroad.
"He has to show he's getting things back on the rails again. I don't know how credible or meaningful his assurance will prove but he knows the international community expects elections next year.
"This is just another gesture and we'll have to see what happens in the next few months. But I think at least he is making the right noises."

Hun Sen has denied he staged a coup against Ranariddh. He said his rival is free to return to Cambodia but would have to face charges for illegally negotiating with the Khmer Rouge and the alleged illegal import of weapons.
Hun Sen has asked members of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party, including some dissidents who broke with the prince in April, to choose a replacement for him as first prime minister.
The elections would be the first since those organised by the United Nations in 1993 with the support of a big peacekeeping operation.
Ranariddh's party won that election but agreed to a power-sharing arrangement with Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party after it threatened to split the country along factional lines.
Analysts in Phnom Penh say Hun Sen would aim to use the election to take control as the country's sole prime minister.

They say that it would be difficult to ensure the elections are free and fair without international supervision and that it was highly doubtful the international community would be willing to fund such a large operation as that in 1993, which cost at least two billion dollars.
